title: Ezekiel 3:1–11
context: The LORD tells the prophet, “Son of man, eat what you find. Eat this scroll, and go, speak to the house of Israel” (3:1). He eats it, and “It was as sweet as honey in my mouth” (3:3), though its contents were lamentations, mourning, and woe (2:10). The LORD then explains the mission: the prophet is not sent to peoples of strange speech, who would listen, but to the house of Israel, who “will not listen to you, for they will not listen to me” (3:5–7). The LORD makes the prophet’s face and forehead hard against theirs, “as a diamond, harder than flint” (3:8–9), and tells him to receive the words in his heart and speak to the exiles “whether they will hear, or whether they will refuse” (3:10–11). The eating is a sign within the vision; compare Jeremiah 15:16 and Revelation 10:9–10, noted only in passing. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: the messenger must first take in the word, and the LORD equips him for a hard audience.

verses.text: He said to me, “Son of man, eat what you find. Eat this scroll, and go, speak to the house of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD commands, “eat what you find. Eat this scroll, and go, speak to the house of Israel.” Arminian readers note that the order matters: the prophet receives before he speaks. Proclamation flows from a word first taken in.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress that the minister must first be fed by the word he delivers. Shared ground: both traditions read the eating as a sign within the vision, showing the prophet’s full identification with the message, rather than as an ordinary meal.

verses.text: So I opened my mouth, and he caused me to eat the scroll.
verses.arminianNotes: “So I opened my mouth, and he caused me to eat the scroll.” Arminian readers note the prophet’s obedient cooperation: he opens his mouth as commanded in 2:8. The LORD provides the word, and the prophet willingly receives it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the LORD “caused me to eat”, stressing divine initiative even in the act of receiving. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as obedience and enabling together, with the prophet’s act and the LORD’s giving both in view.

verses.text: He said to me, “Son of man, eat this scroll that I give you and fill your belly and your bowels with it.” Then I ate it. It was as sweet as honey in my mouth.
verses.arminianNotes: The scroll “was as sweet as honey in my mouth”, though its message is lament. Arminian readers note that the word of the LORD is good even when it brings hard news. Compare Jeremiah 15:16, where the prophet eats the LORD’s words and finds them a joy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the sweetness of God’s word to the one who receives it, even when it pronounces judgment (compare Psalm 19:10). Shared ground: both traditions note the bitterness that follows in 3:14, and mention the sweet scroll of Revelation 10:9–10 only in passing.

verses.text: He said to me, “Son of man, go to the house of Israel, and speak my words to them.
verses.arminianNotes: “Son of man, go to the house of Israel, and speak my words to them.” Arminian readers note the emphasis on “my words”. The prophet is a messenger, and the people’s response will be to the LORD’s own words, not merely to one man’s opinions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress that the prophet’s authority lies in delivering the LORD’s words faithfully. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as restating the commission of 2:7, and both see the messenger bound to speak what he has received.

verses.text: For you are not sent to a people of a strange speech and of a hard language, but to the house of Israel—
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet is “not sent to a people of a strange speech and of a hard language”. Arminian readers note the irony. Language is no barrier with Israel; the barrier lies in the hearers’ hearts, not in any difficulty of understanding.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the problem located in the will and heart rather than the intellect. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as preparing for 3:7, where the refusal of the house of Israel is traced to their refusal of the LORD himself.

verses.text: not to many peoples of a strange speech and of a hard language, whose words you can’t understand. Surely, if I sent you to them, they would listen to you.
verses.arminianNotes: “Surely, if I sent you to them, they would listen to you.” Arminian readers, some drawing on the idea of middle knowledge, see the LORD knowing how free people would respond in other circumstances. Compare Matthew 11:21 and the treatment at 1 Samuel 23:12.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm that the LORD knows what would happen in circumstances that never occur, commonly grounding that knowledge in his own wisdom and decree. Shared ground: both read the verse as a rebuke to Israel; compare the treatment at 1 Samuel 23:12.

verses.text: But the house of Israel will not listen to you, for they will not listen to me; for all the house of Israel are obstinate and hard-hearted.
verses.arminianNotes: “But the house of Israel will not listen to you, for they will not listen to me”. Arminian readers note that the LORD foreknows the refusal without causing it; the people are “obstinate and hard-hearted” by their own persistence. Compare the treatment at Deuteronomy 31:21.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the refusal as real and culpable, while holding that the LORD’s knowledge of it rests in his sovereign purpose. Shared ground: both traditions see rejection of the messenger as rejection of the LORD, and both point to the treatment at Deuteronomy 31:21.

verses.text: Behold, I have made your face hard against their faces, and your forehead hard against their foreheads.
verses.arminianNotes: “I have made your face hard against their faces”. Arminian readers note that the LORD equips the prophet for opposition. The people’s hardness will be met by a prophet made firm, not by a softened message.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s sovereign strengthening of his servant for an obstinate audience. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a promise of resilience, matching the people’s obstinacy in 3:7 with the prophet’s God-given firmness.

verses.text: I have made your forehead as a diamond, harder than flint. Don’t be afraid of them, neither be dismayed at their looks, though they are a rebellious house.”
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet’s forehead is made “as a diamond, harder than flint”, and he is again told not to be afraid. Arminian readers note the pastoral care in the repeated command. The LORD anticipates the prophet’s fear and answers it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s provision for his servant in a hostile setting. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as joining strength and comfort, and both see the refrain “they are a rebellious house” shaping the whole commission (compare 2:5–8).

verses.text: Moreover he said to me, “Son of man, receive in your heart and hear with your ears all my words that I speak to you.
verses.arminianNotes: “Son of man, receive in your heart and hear with your ears all my words that I speak to you.” Arminian readers note that the prophet must first take the word to heart. He is not a mere channel; the message must take hold of him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress that the minister must be shaped by the word before he speaks it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as restating in plain terms the meaning of the eaten scroll, with heart and ears both engaged.

verses.text: Go to them of the captivity, to the children of your people, and speak to them, and tell them, ‘This is what the Lord GOD says,’ whether they will hear, or whether they will refuse.”
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet is sent to “them of the captivity, to the children of your people”. Arminian readers note that the mission is now specified: the exiles, his own people. The call to speak stands “whether they will hear, or whether they will refuse.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the commission focused on the exiles and the prophet’s solidarity with them. Shared ground: both traditions read the repeated hear-or-refuse formula (compare 2:5 and 2:7) as setting the prophet’s faithfulness apart from the hearers’ response.
